Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

off preposition and adverb

off a surface: fall off, take off, get off

also off the coast of, off (of an island)

classical

Vulg. Mt. 15.27: mīcīs quae cadunt dē mēnsā
Plaut. Cas. 931: dēcidō dē lectō praecipes

dē (+ ablative)

preposition with the ablative · Wiktionary

off, down from

From a surface, usually downward: dē mēnsā, off the table; dē lectō, off the bed; dē digitō, off a finger.

Other words

  • dētrahō, dētrahere, dētrāxī, dētractum — pull off, take off

    verb, third conjugation, with dē or ex + ablative, or a dative of the person · classical · Ter. Heaut. 650–651: dē digitō ānulum dētrahō · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    English “off” is often a Latin prefix: dē- (dēcidere, fall off; dētrahere, pull off; dēscendere, get off), ab- (abīre, go off; auferre, take off, carry off), ex- (exuere, take off clothes: see take off).

  • ē, ex (+ ablative) — off (getting down from)

    preposition with the ablative · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 34: ex equō nōn dēscendere · Wiktionary

    Ex equō dēscendere, get off a horse; ē nāve ēgredī, get off a ship.

Examples

  • nam et catellī edunt dē mīcīs quae cadunt dē mēnsā dominōrum suōrum

    for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall off their masters’ tableVulg. Mt. 15.27

  • dēcidō dē lectō praecipes: subsilit, optundit ōs mihi

    I tumble headlong off the couch; he jumps on me and punches me in the facePlaut. Cas. 931

  • 1Ter. Heaut. 650–651: the Perseus text prints annulum; we give anulum, the spelling of Lewis & Short’s citation and headword.

    dē digitō ānulum dētrahō1

    I take the ring off my fingerTer. Heaut. 650–651

  • tam ineptum erit quam flēre quod arboribus amoenīs et domum tuam ōrnantibus dēcidant folia

    it will be as silly as weeping because the leaves fall off the lovely trees that adorn your houseSen. Ep. 104.11

  • ante Italiam

    off (the coast of) ItalyTraupman 353

See also on, from, take off, climb down, away.
